note: Every entry was found and its abstract (or full text, see "read") read by a research agent on the access date. DOIs were re-checked against Crossref by script; arXiv IDs against the arXiv API.

sources.title: Speech Accent Archive
sources.authors: Weinberger, S.
sources.accents: ~2,000 speakers of 200+ native languages/L1 backgrounds reading the same English passage; labelled by L1 language; native-American-English speakers included as reference
sources.measured: Same short read paragraph per speaker, designed for accent strength research; used by Wieling et al. 2014 and Bartelds et al. 2020/2022
sources.finding: The canonical L2-accent corpus for phonetic-distance work: native-likeness ratings on a subset correlate r=-0.81 with phonetic edit distance and r=-0.71 with MFCC+DTW acoustic distance. Download via OSF after accepting terms.

sources.title: L2-ARCTIC: A Non-native English Speech Corpus
sources.authors: Zhao, G.; Mou, W.; Chen, S.; Zhu, H.; Saghir, H.; AlBadrashiny, M.; Kurmanji, M.; Liu, Y.; Chitkara, N.; Rudzicz, F.; Jin, Z.
sources.accents: 10 non-native English speakers from 6 L1s (Arabic x2, Hindi x2, Korean x2, Mandarin x3, Spanish x1)
sources.measured: Read speech, ~150 utterances per speaker, ~1 h each; utterances manually annotated for mispronunciations at phone level
sources.finding: Small but deeply annotated L2 corpus; standard testbed for mispronunciation detection (used by Yan 2021, Baranwal 2022, Sara 2026, He 2026). Licence CC BY-NC 4.0 — research only, no commercial use.

sources.title: CMU ARCTIC speech database
sources.authors: Kominek, J.; Black, A.W.
sources.accents: 18 speakers: 7 US English (mostly), plus Scottish, Indian, Canadian, German-accented, etc., paired male/female per accent
sources.measured: ~1132 phonetically balanced sentences per speaker (~1 h each), studio-quality read speech at 16 kHz
sources.finding: Classic TTS corpus with several non-native English accents. Licence allows research and commercial use with restrictions (BSD-style; verify current terms at festvox.org).

sources.title: Mozilla Common Voice (English v27.0)
sources.authors: Ardila, R.; Branson, M.; Davis, K.; et al. (Mozilla Foundation)
sources.accents: Self-reported accent field in free text since mid-2022: ~907k speakers, ~15,341 unique accent entries (per ACM study); English subset incl. scotland 69,286 clips / 272 speakers in v27
sources.measured: Read sentences from a fixed prompt set; validated clips; English v27.0 is 88.43 GB
sources.finding: Largest crowd-sourced labelled-English-accent resource. Licence CC0-1.0 via Mozilla Data Collective. Terms forbid re-hosting/re-sharing and forbid attempts to identify speakers.

sources.title: CORAAL — Corpus of Regional American English
sources.authors: Gunter, S.; Kendall, T.; Farrington, C.
sources.accents: American regional varieties: Atlanta, Bay Area, Charlotte, Erie, Evanston, Herron, Huntsville, Memphis, New Orleans, Raleigh, Rochester, South Atlanta, Washington DC; 220+ speakers
sources.measured: Spontaneous sociolinguistic interviews/conversation, ~1M words total
sources.finding: The main US regional-dialect speech corpus. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — non-commercial share-alike. Direct tar.gz download.

sources.title: IViE — International Variation in English
sources.authors: Griffiths, P.
sources.venue: Corpus hosted by Queen Mary University of London
sources.accents: Urban British Isles Englishes: London, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle, Nottingham, Cardiff, Edinburgh, Belfast
sources.measured: ~36 h spontaneous conversation from ~120 speakers across 9 urban dialect areas
sources.finding: Standard British-urban-dialect corpus. Free for academic research and teaching only via registration; not for commercial use.

sources.title: Atlas of North American English (ANAE) speech data
sources.authors: Labov, W.; Ash, S.; Boberg, C.
sources.venue: book: The Atlas of North American English; data from Telsur project
sources.accents: US and Canadian regional vowel systems; ~50 cities, thousands of speakers
sources.measured: Spontaneous sociolinguistic interviews analysed for vowel formants (F1/F2), chains of vowel shifts; acoustic rather than full audio corpus publicly
sources.finding: Source of the canonical Northern-Cities Shift / regional vowel map; most data is public formant/text data rather than raw audio. Use for accent-typology charts, not as training audio.

sources.title: Nationwide Speech Project (NSP) corpus
sources.authors: Hillenbrand, J.; American Dialect Society
sources.accents: 60 speakers from 6 US dialect regions (inland north, south, New England, midland, west, etc.)
sources.measured: Spontaneous conversation and read speech, ~60 h
sources.finding: Classic US dialect corpus. LDC licence; LDC terms state corpus is 'not available for commercial purposes' — commercial use requires negotiation.

sources.title: VCTK Corpus
sources.authors: Yamagishi, J.; Veaux, C.; MacDonald, K.
sources.accents: 110 speakers of various English accents (with accent labels per speaker)
sources.measured: ~44 h read speech (newspaper sentences), 48 kHz studio quality
sources.finding: Standard multi-speaker TTS corpus; accent labels included. Licence CC BY 4.0 — commercial use allowed; speakers' moral rights: no derogatory use.

sources.title: GLOBE English TTS corpus
sources.authors: Mushan W.; (GLOBE project, globecorpus.github.io)
sources.accents: 164 English accent labels derived from Common Voice self-reports
sources.measured: 535 h, 23,519 speakers, derived/cleaned from Mozilla Common Voice; designed for TTS and ASR with accent labels
sources.finding: Largest ready-made multi-accent English TTS corpus. Licence CC0-1.0. Check HF model card for redistribution terms.

sources.title: EdAcc — Edinburgh International Accents of English Corpus
sources.authors: Sanabria, R.; Bogoychev, N.; Markl, N.; Carmantini, A.; Klejch, O.; Bell, P.
sources.accents: ~25 accent classes, 29 L1 labels, 120 speakers in ~62 speaker groups (Hugging Face release)
sources.measured: ~40 h of dyadic video calls between friends (spontaneous conversational)
sources.finding: Modern conversational accented-English benchmark; CC BY-SA licence per corpus page; Hugging Face distribution.

sources.title: speechocean762
sources.authors: Zhang, J.; Zhang, Z.; Wang, Y.; Yan, Z.; Song, Q.; Huang, Y.; Li, K.; Povey, D.; Wang, Y.
sources.accents: 250 Mandarin-L1 speakers (125 children, 125 adults)
sources.measured: 5000 read English utterances, sentence/word/phoneme expert scores from 5 annotators
sources.finding: Standard pronunciation-assessment benchmark. Licence CC BY 4.0 — free for commercial and non-commercial use.

sources.title: LibriSpeech / LibriTTS
sources.authors: Panayotov, V.; Chen, G.; Povey, D.; Khudanpur, S.
sources.accents: US English audiobooks (LibriVox); no accent labels — speaker IDs only
sources.measured: LibriSpeech ~1000 h read speech; LibriTTS ~585 h with speaker IDs
sources.finding: Both CC BY 4.0. Valuable as the 'native American' reference class in accent-ID systems, but no accent metadata — cannot be split by accent without external labels.

sources.title: AccentDB
sources.authors: Joglekar, S.; et al. (THST IIT Bombay)
sources.accents: 9 accent classes in core set (4 Indian non-native + 5 native incl. metropolitan Indian); accentdb_extended with 19,111 files
sources.measured: Connected/sentence read speech and spontaneous utterances
sources.finding: Indian-English accent classification dataset. Licence CC BY-NC 4.0 — non-commercial only.

sources.title: Indic TIMIT
sources.authors: Kumar, A.; et al. (IIT Madras)
sources.accents: Indian English spoken by native speakers of several Indian languages
sources.measured: Phonetically balanced read sentences per speaker
sources.finding: Indic-accented read speech. Access via LDC/institutional agreement — fee/licence terms; verify current terms before use.

sources.title: TIMIT
sources.authors: Garofolo, J.S.; Lamel, L.F.; Fisher, W.M.; Fiscus, J.G.; Santen, J.P.; Stern, R.M.
sources.accents: 630 speakers across 8 US dialect regions (dr1 New England … dr8 Army Brat)
sources.measured: Read phonetically-balanced speech with hand-checked phonetic transcription
sources.finding: The classic dialect-labelled corpus. LDC licence; paid ($250 non-member / $150 reduced member at catalog time). The dialect regions are coarse (speaker dialect region self/analyst-labelled), not accent recordings.

sources.title: Buckeye Corpus of Conversational Speech
sources.authors: Pitt, M.A.; Johnson, K.; Hume, E.; Kiesling, S.; Raymond, W.
sources.accents: 40 speakers from Columbus, Ohio — effectively one urban US accent
sources.measured: ~40 h spontaneous conversation, ~1 h per speaker
sources.finding: Freely available for non-commercial use via registration form; commercial use unclear/negotiable. Only one dialect, so limited value for multi-accent modelling but useful as native-US conversational speech.

sources.title: Scottish Corpus of Texts and Speech (SCOTS)
sources.authors: SCOTS project (University of Glasgow / Scottish Corpus of Texts and Speech)
sources.accents: Scottish varieties: written corpus plus spoken corpus from across Scotland
sources.measured: Mixed written and spoken texts; spoken part contains read and spontaneous speech
sources.finding: Primary source for Scottish English language/accent research. Registration/login; licence terms academic, non-commercial — verify before commercial use.

sources.title: Sounds of the City (SoTC) — Glasgow speech corpus
sources.authors: Stuart-Smith, J.; Mearns, L.; et al.
sources.venue: University of Glasgow / Queen Mary University of London project
sources.accents: Glasgow (and other Scottish city) speech, multiple age/socioeconomic groups
sources.measured: Fieldwork recordings of spontaneous speech (interviews, conversation)
sources.finding: The Glasgow-accent corpus behind the 'Sounds of the City' project. Public access is limited/arranged through the project; UNVERIFIED whether downloadable audio is available — likely restricted academic access.

sources.title: International Dialects of English Archive (IDEA)
sources.authors: Kirk, J.; Anderson, A.
sources.accents: ~127 English varieties worldwide, speakers from many countries
sources.measured: Each speaker reads a standard text (two short passages) — read speech
sources.finding: Same-text read speech from ~800+ speakers; excellent for accent typology. Access via website; usage terms restrict commercial reuse — check terms before any commercial use.

sources.title: British Library Sounds / Accents and Dialects (Evolving English)
sources.authors: British Library
sources.accents: UK regional and heritage accents; dialect recordings across Britain
sources.measured: Spontaneous speech interviews/dialect recordings
sources.finding: Some collections public with download; many under non-commercial or request-access terms; UK accent focus.

sources.title: Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL predecessor: Corpus of African American Language / DCA)
sources.authors: Kendall, T.; Wolfram, W.
sources.accents: African American English varieties across the US
sources.measured: Spontaneous conversation recordings
sources.finding: Research access terms (academic, request-based); non-commercial restrictions apply.

sources.title: ICE — International Corpus of English (spoken components)
sources.authors: Greenbaum, S.; Nelson, G.
sources.accents: National/variety components: Indian, Singapore, Philippines, Canada, Hong Kong, New Zealand, etc., ~1M words each
sources.measured: Mixed spoken (private/public dialogue, lectures) and written; spoken parts partly transcribed with audio available for some components
sources.finding: Audio access varies by national component; generally academic licence; useful for post-colonial English varieties.

sources.title: Toronto English corpora (Toronto Dominance/Variety Corpus etc.)
sources.authors: Rosenfelder, I.
sources.venue: U of Toronto Dept. of Linguistics
sources.accents: Canadian English varieties incl. Toronto and ethnolects (e.g. Cantonese-accented, Portuguese-accented English)
sources.measured: Controlled word-list + sentence read speech
sources.finding: Free for research; sizes are modest (word lists/sentence sets per speaker group). Key for Toronto English targets.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED: the listed URL returned HTTP 404 on 2026-11-15; corpus name and access terms not confirmed.

sources.title: AESRC2020 — Accented English Speech Recognition Challenge data
sources.authors: AESRC2020 organising committee (Nexdata / DataTang)
sources.accents: 10 accents by country of recording (Chinese, American, British, Korean, Japanese, Russian, Indian, Portuguese, Spanish, Canadian); 8 with 20 h labelled train each
sources.measured: 160 h labelled training (20 h per accent) + 20 h unlabelled test; phone-recorded read speech
sources.finding: The standard accent-ID benchmark. Distribution via commercial data vendor — paid commercial licence; academic use arrangements vary.

sources.title: Hugging Face 'accented English' subsets / accent-classification datasets
sources.authors: Various community uploads
sources.venue: huggingface.co datasets (e.g. mohitg/accent-classification, accent-classification subsets of Common Voice)
sources.accents: Various: Common Voice-derived accent splits, EdAcc subsets, GLOBE
sources.measured: Varies by upload — many are small curated subsets of Common Voice with accent labels
sources.finding: Convenient for prototyping, but licences are inherited from the source corpus; several are redistributions of non-redistributable data — UNVERIFIED compliance; prefer downloading source corpora directly.

sources.title: L2-ARCTIC / Speech Accent Archive mirrors
sources.authors: Various (unofficial mirrors)
sources.accents: Same as originals
sources.measured: Mirrors of the official corpora
sources.finding: Mirrors may violate licence terms (Common Voice explicitly forbids re-hosting). Use official download channels only.

sources.title: The Accented English Speech Recognition Challenge 2020: Open Datasets, Tracks, Baselines, Results and Methods
sources.authors: Shi, X.; Yu, F.; Lu, Y.; Liang, Y.; Feng, Q.; Wang, D.; Qian, Y.; Xie, L.
sources.accents: 10 English accents by country of recording: Chinese, American, British, Korean, Japanese, Russian, Indian, Portuguese, Spanish, Canadian
sources.measured: Accent recognition track (track 1) and accented speech recognition track (track 2); 160 h labelled training data (20 h per accent for 8 accents), 20 h unlabelled test incl. 2 unseen accents
sources.finding: Defines the standard benchmark: 180 h total, phone-recorded read speech. Winning accent-ID system reached 83.63% average accuracy on the challenge test set (reported in Huang et al. 2021). Baseline systems and per-accent WER tables are published in the paper.

sources.title: AISPEECH-SJTU accent identification system for the Accented English Speech Recognition Challenge
sources.authors: Huang, H.; Xiang, X.; Yang, Y.; Ma, R.; Qian, Y.
sources.accents: 8 country-level English accents in AESRC2020 training data (China, US, UK, Korea, Japan, Russia, India, Portugal)
sources.measured: Accent ID with ASR phone posteriorgram (PPG) features, TTS-based data augmentation, test-time augmentation and embedding fusion
sources.finding: Winning AESRC2020 track-1 system: 83.63% average accuracy on the challenge evaluation data, 'ahead of the others by more than 10% in absolute terms'. Training used 160 h accented data plus auxiliary LibriSpeech.

sources.title: Improving Accent Identification and Accented Speech Recognition Under a Framework of Self-supervised Learning
sources.authors: Deng, K.; Cao, S.; Ma, L.
sources.accents: 8 English accents in AESRC2020 (English, America, China, Japan, Russia, India, Portugal, Korea)
sources.measured: Self-supervised pre-training (wav2vec 2.0 style) on 960 h unlabelled LibriSpeech, fine-tuned on AESRC2020; standard-deviation-constraint loss for accent ID plus accent-dependent ASR
sources.finding: Accent-dependent ASR system 'significantly ahead of the AESRC2020 baseline' with 6.5% relative WER reduction vs the accent-independent system. Shows self-supervised features transfer to accent ID/ASR.

sources.title: CommonAccent: Exploring Large Acoustic Pretrained Models for Accent Classification Based on Common Voice
sources.authors: Zuluaga-Gomez, J.; Ahmed, S.; Visockas, D.; Subakan, C.
sources.accents: English accents labelled in Mozilla Common Voice 7.0 (plus Italian, German, Spanish in multilingual experiments)
sources.measured: ECAPA-TDNN and Wav2Vec 2.0/XLSR classifiers (SpeechBrain recipe) on Common Voice accent labels; t-SNE analysis of embedding structure
sources.finding: New state of the art for English accent classification 'with as high as 95% accuracy'. Embeddings show clustering by phonological similarity. Speaker-independent split details not stated in abstract (flag: verify).

sources.title: The Edinburgh International Accents of English Corpus: Towards the Democratization of English ASR (EdAcc)
sources.authors: Sanabria, R.; Bogoychev, N.; Markl, N.; Carmantini, A.; Klejch, O.; Bell, P.
sources.accents: Wide range of L1 and L2 English varieties; ~25 accent classes and 29 L1 labels in released metadata (62 speaker groups in HF release)
sources.measured: ~40 h of dyadic video-call conversations between friends with linguistic background profiles; benchmark of public and commercial ASR models
sources.finding: Best public model (trained on 680k h) gets 19.7% average WER on EdAcc vs 2.7% on clean US English read speech; biggest drops on Indian, Jamaican and Nigerian English. Spontaneous conversational domain — harder than read-speech benchmarks.

sources.title: Improved Accent Classification Combining Phonetic Vowels with Acoustic Features
sources.authors: Ge, Z.
sources.accents: 7 major accented-English types in the Foreign Accented English (FAE) corpus
sources.measured: GMM-UBM classifier on normalized PLP features + phonetic vowel information, PCA + HLDA
sources.finding: 54% classification accuracy with test segments as short as 20 seconds — a mid-2010s classical baseline, far below modern embedding classifiers but with tiny data needs.

sources.title: Revisiting Accent Classification with DistilHuBERT: Speaker-Disjoint Evaluation and Cross-Corpus Generalization
sources.authors: He, X.; Beigi, H.
sources.accents: L2-ARCTIC accents (Hindi, Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic L1s) plus multiple external English accent datasets
sources.measured: DistilHuBERT accent classification under file-level vs speaker-disjoint splits; cross-corpus evaluation; teacher-student pseudo-labelling
sources.finding: Large gap between in-corpus and external evaluation: file-level evaluation 'substantially overestimates performance', speaker-disjoint evaluation is the realistic estimate. Models trained on external data alone do not reliably generalize to L2-ARCTIC. Key warning for anyone reporting accent-ID accuracy.

sources.title: The XMUSPEECH System for Accented English Automatic Speech Recognition
sources.authors: Tong, F.; Li, T.; Liao, D.; Xia, S.; Li, S.; Hong, Q.; Li, L.
sources.accents: 8 country-level English accents in AESRC2020
sources.measured: Comparison of i-vector and x-vector embeddings (speaker and accent variants) as extra features for accented ASR; TDNN-LSTM acoustic model + LM rescoring
sources.finding: x-vector embedding outperformed i-vector embedding; accent embeddings improved accented ASR with relative WER improvements of 40.7% (dev) and 35.7% (eval) vs baseline. Shows i/x-vector embeddings carry usable accent information, not just speaker information.

sources.title: Probing for Phonology in Self-Supervised Speech Representations: A Case Study on Accent Perception
sources.authors: Venkateswaran, N.; Tang, K.; Wayland, R.
sources.accents: Indian English vs American English (Hindi-background speakers, CSLU Foreign Accented English corpus)
sources.measured: Layer-wise probing of Wav2Vec2-BERT and WavLM representations against phonological feature probabilities and native-speaker accent ratings
sources.finding: Accent strength is best predicted by a subset of pretrained features where perceptually salient phonological features (contrasting expected American vs realized Indian segments) get prominent weighting; segment distances from American/Indian baselines strongly associate with accent-rating odds. SSL representations encode accent-relevant phonological detail usable for interpretable scoring.

sources.title: Mispronunciation detection using self-supervised speech representations
sources.authors: Vidal, J.; Riera, P.; Ferrer, L.
sources.accents: L2 English: L2-ARCTIC (5 L1s) and EpaDB (Spanish L1)
sources.measured: SSL representations (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT etc.) for mispronunciation detection; phone-recognition vs target-task downstream training
sources.finding: Downstream model trained directly on the target task performs best; most upstream SSL models perform similarly for mispronunciation detection. Phone-level error detection on L2-ARCTIC and EpaDB.

sources.title: Evaluating Logit-Based GOP Scores for Mispronunciation Detection
sources.authors: Parikh, A.K.; Tejedor-Garcia, C.; Cucchiarini, C.; Strik, H.
sources.accents: L2 English: Dutch and Mandarin speakers
sources.measured: Logit-based vs probability-based Goodness of Pronunciation scores; classification performance and correlation with human ratings
sources.finding: Logit-based GOP outperforms probability-based GOP in classification; the maximum-logit GOP 'shows the strongest alignment with human perception'. Hybrid GOP methods combining probability and logit features suggested.

sources.title: Segmentation-free Goodness of Pronunciation
sources.authors: Cao, X.; Fan, Z.; Svendsen, T.; Salvi, G.
sources.accents: L2 English: speechocean762 and CMU Kids
sources.measured: Self-alignment GOP (GOP-SA) and segmentation-free GOP (GOP-SF) for CTC-trained ASR models; theoretical normalization across acoustic-model peakiness
sources.finding: Removes the forced-alignment dependency of classic GOP so modern CTC acoustic models (incl. weakly-supervised multilingual ones) can be used for mispronunciation detection. No headline correlation number in abstract.

sources.title: Goodness-of-pronunciation without phoneme time alignment
sources.authors: Wong, J.H.M.; Chen, N.F.
sources.accents: English (speechocean762) and Tamil (low-resource)
sources.measured: Phoneme posteriors from frame-asynchronous weakly-supervised ASR via phoneme confusion network; cross-attention fusion of phoneme and frame features, no forced alignment
sources.finding: Performs comparably to standard frame-synchronous GOP features on speechocean762 and extends pronunciation scoring to low-resource languages where forced alignment is unavailable.

sources.title: ASR-Free Pronunciation Assessment
sources.authors: Cheng, S.; Liu, Z.; Li, L.; Tang, Z.; Wang, D.; Zheng, T.F.
sources.accents: Japanese L2 English (ERJ dataset)
sources.measured: Scoring from marginal distribution of raw speech signals without ASR; combined with GOP to fix phone-competition problem
sources.finding: ASR-free score combined with GOP beats the GOP baseline on ERJ. A non-ASR path to pronunciation scoring using only target-language speech statistics.

sources.title: Improving pronunciation assessment via ordinal regression with anchored reference samples
sources.authors: Su, B.; Mao, S.; Soong, F.; Xia, Y.; Tien, J.; Wu, Z.
sources.accents: Mandarin L1 English learners (Microsoft mTutor ESL dataset)
sources.measured: average GOP (aGOP) and confusion GOP (cGOP) features with ordinal regression and anchored reference samples
sources.finding: 26.9% relative improvement in Pearson correlation with human ratings over conventional GOP averaging; performance described as 'at a human-parity level or better than human raters'. Direct evidence that simple GOP post-processing can match human scoring.

sources.title: Phone-level pronunciation scoring and assessment for interactive language learning
sources.authors: Witt, S.M.; Young, S.J.
sources.accents: Non-native English (mixed L1 backgrounds, specially recorded database)
sources.measured: Original Goodness of Pronunciation (GOP): likelihood-based phone score from HMM/DNN acoustic model posterior vs canonical phone, with per-phone thresholds from native confidence and human rejection stats
sources.finding: The canonical GOP paper: likelihood-based phone-level scoring 'can achieve usable performance' and improved with native-language and expected-error modelling. Basis of nearly all later pronunciation scoring.

sources.title: speechocean762: An Open-Source Non-native English Speech Corpus For Pronunciation Assessment
sources.authors: Zhang, J.; Zhang, Z.; Wang, Y.; Yan, Z.; Song, Q.; Huang, Y.; Li, K.; Povey, D.; Wang, Y.
sources.accents: 250 non-native English speakers, all Mandarin L1 (half children)
sources.measured: 5000 English utterances with sentence/word/phoneme-level scores from five independent expert annotators; Kaldi baseline
sources.finding: Standard benchmark for pronunciation assessment with multi-aspect human scores; free for commercial and non-commercial use (CC BY 4.0).

sources.title: Transformer-Based Multi-Aspect Multi-Granularity Non-Native English Speaker Pronunciation Assessment (GOPT)
sources.authors: Gong, Y.; Chen, Z.; Chu, I.-H.; Chang, P.; Glass, J.
sources.accents: Mandarin L1 English learners (speechocean762)
sources.measured: GOP-feature Transformer with multi-task learning for accuracy/fluency/completeness/prosody at phoneme/word/sentence levels; public LibriSpeech ASR acoustic model
sources.finding: Best results on speechocean762 using only a public Librispeech-trained ASR model — evidence that off-the-shelf native-English ASR features suffice for strong pronunciation scoring.

sources.title: Zero-Shot Automatic Pronunciation Assessment
sources.authors: Liu, H.; Shi, M.; Wang, Y.
sources.accents: Mandarin L1 English learners (speechocean762)
sources.measured: HuBERT features with masking, k-means tokenization, and a scoring module counting wrongly recovered tokens; no scored training data
sources.finding: Comparable Pearson correlation to supervised regression baselines on speechocean762 and beats non-regression baselines — scoring possible without any labelled learner data.

sources.title: MultiPA: A Multi-task Speech Pronunciation Assessment Model for Open Response Scenarios
sources.authors: Chen, Y.-W.; Yu, Z.; Hirschberg, J.
sources.accents: Non-native English, open-response speech (new out-of-domain set collected)
sources.measured: Multi-task model predicting sentence accuracy, fluency, prosody and word accuracy for spontaneous responses
sources.finding: State-of-the-art on existing in-domain sets and generalizes to a new out-of-domain open-response dataset; multi-task learning across aspects helps.

sources.title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
sources.authors: Sara, S.F.A.; Chowdhury, S.A.
sources.accents: speechocean762 (Mandarin L1) and L2-ARCTIC (5 L1s)
sources.measured: SSL-encoded discrete tokens + K-means codebook; token language model surprisal on native speech; Text2DUnit-DTW alignment with reference text
sources.finding: PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 on speechocean762 with transcript guidance, 'near supervised baselines', trained only on native speech; consistent gains cross-dataset on L2-ARCTIC. A lightweight phone-feasible candidate.

sources.title: Maximum F1-score training for end-to-end mispronunciation detection and diagnosis of L2 English speech
sources.authors: Yan, B.-C.; Jiang, S.-W.F.; Chao, F.-A.; Chen, B.
sources.accents: L2 English: L2-ARCTIC (Hindi, Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic L1s)
sources.measured: End-to-end MDD with discriminative F1-maximizing objective vs cross-entropy; compared to GOP baseline
sources.finding: Considerable F1 improvements over state-of-the-art E2E MDD approaches and the celebrated GOP method on L2-ARCTIC. Direct phone-error detection beats likelihood scoring when labelled L2 data exists.

sources.title: Improved Mispronunciation detection system using a hybrid CTC-ATT based approach for L2 English speakers
sources.authors: Baranwal, N.; Chilaka, S.
sources.accents: L2 English speakers
sources.measured: Hybrid CTC/attention mispronunciation detection vs GMM-HMM and DNN-HMM GOP approaches
sources.finding: Reviews the GOP lineage (GMM-HMM/DNN-HMM posterior likelihood) and proposes a hybrid CTC-ATT detector; notes consensus that pronunciation teaching should target intelligibility rather than native-likeness.

sources.title: DTW-SiameseNet: Dynamic Time Warped Siamese Network for Mispronunciation Detection and Correction
sources.authors: Anantha, R.; Bhasin, K.; de la Parra Aguilar, D.; Vashisht, P.; Williamson, B.; Chappidi, S.
sources.accents: Multi-lingual/dialect TTS named-entity mispronunciation (not strictly accent scoring; included for DTW-based comparison)
sources.measured: Siamese network over DTW-aligned speech embeddings for mispronunciation detection and correction without ground-truth pronunciation annotation
sources.finding: DTW over learned embeddings detects mispronounced named entities precisely without expensive pronunciation annotation — direct descendant of the DTW-distance idea used in Sound Local's pitch scoring.

sources.title: Automatic Pronunciation Assessment - A Review
sources.authors: El Kheir, Y.; Ali, A.; Chowdhury, S.A.
sources.accents: L2 learners across languages (survey)
sources.measured: Taxonomy of phonemic and prosodic pronunciation assessment methods, challenges, resources
sources.finding: Updated survey of pronunciation assessment: segmental (GOP-family) and prosodic (duration, pitch, rhythm) methods, open problems in data scarcity and multi-aspect scoring.

sources.title: A New Acoustic-Based Pronunciation Distance Measure
sources.authors: Bartelds, M.; Richter, C.; Liberman, M.; Wieling, M.
sources.accents: Non-native English accents vs native American English (Speech Accent Archive)
sources.measured: Word-based acoustic distances on MFCCs with speaker-based cepstral mean/variance normalization, computed with dynamic time warping; no phonetic transcription needed
sources.finding: Strong correlation r = -0.71 (p < 0.0001) with native-likeness judgments of >1,100 raters, only slightly below the transcription-based r = -0.77; sensitive to segmental, intonational and durational differences but not immune to recording-device differences.

sources.title: Neural representations for modeling variation in speech
sources.authors: Bartelds, M.; de Vries, W.; Sanal, F.; Richter, C.; Liberman, M.; Wieling, M.
sources.accents: Non-native English vs native American English; Norwegian dialects
sources.measured: Acoustic embeddings from self-supervised neural models (Transformers best); word-based pronunciation distances compared with human similarity judgments; layer analysis
sources.finding: Transformer-based SSL representations match human perception of pronunciation differences better than phonetic-transcription and MFCC-based approaches; best features come from middle hidden layers, not the final layer; representations capture intonation and duration that discrete phonetic symbols cannot.

sources.title: Quantifying Language Variation Acoustically with Few Resources
sources.authors: Bartelds, M.; Wieling, M.
sources.accents: 100+ Dutch regional dialects (plus three other regional languages)
sources.measured: wav2vec 2.0 / XLSR-53 embeddings + dynamic time warping for pairwise pronunciation distances; clustering vs gold standard
sources.finding: Acoustic model distances beat traditional transcription-based dialect distances with no phonetic transcriptions; best with multilingual XLSR-53 fine-tuned on the target language; 'on the basis of only six seconds of speech, the resulting clustering closely matches the gold standard' — very little audio needed per speaker.

sources.title: Measuring Foreign Accent Strength in English: Validating Levenshtein Distance as a Measure
sources.authors: Wieling, M.; Bloem, J.; Mignella, K.; Timmermeister, M.; Nerbonne, J.
sources.accents: Non-native English accents vs native American English (Speech Accent Archive)
sources.measured: Modified Levenshtein (string edit) distance on phonetic transcriptions of the same elicitation paragraph; validated against human native-likeness ratings
sources.finding: Correlates strongly with average 'native-like' judgments of >1,000 native US raters: r = -0.81 (p < 0.001). Phonetic-transcription distance is the classic validated accent-strength metric, but requires manual transcription.
sources.doi_check: title matches Crossref (Crossref omits the subtitle)

sources.title: Disentangling accent from comprehensibility
sources.authors: Trofimovich, P.; Isaacs, T.
sources.accents: 40 native French speakers of English (L2)
sources.measured: 19 speech measures (segmental, prosodic, temporal, lexical, grammatical) related to accent and comprehensibility ratings by 60 novice raters and 3 experienced teachers
sources.finding: Accent is uniquely related to phonology — rhythm, segmental and syllable-structure accuracy — while comprehensibility is chiefly linked to grammatical accuracy and lexical richness. Accent scoring should therefore weight phonological/phonetic detail, not grammar.

sources.title: Modeling Perceptions of the Accentedness and Comprehensibility of L2 Speech: The Role of Speaking Rate
sources.authors: Munro, M.J.; Derwing, T.M.
sources.accents: English L2 users from a variety of L1 backgrounds
sources.measured: Two experiments relating speaking rate to accentedness and comprehensibility judgments; rate manipulated with compression-expansion software
sources.finding: Significant curvilinear relationship: listeners rate slightly-faster-than-typical L2 speech highest; very fast and very slow speech rated lower. Speaking rate alone shifts perceived accentedness — any accent score must control for rate or it will mislead.

sources.title: Suprasegmental Measures of Accentedness and Judgments of Language Learner Proficiency in Oral English
sources.authors: Kang, O.; Rubin, D.; Pickering, L.
sources.accents: 26 iBT TOEFL examinees (L2 English)
sources.measured: Instrumental suprasegmental measures (speech rate, pause, intonation/pitch) via CSL; proficiency and comprehensibility judgments by 188 raters
sources.finding: Suprasegmental measures collectively accounted for 50% of the variance in oral proficiency and comprehensibility ratings. Pitch, rhythm and pausing carry half the perceptual signal of 'how accented' speech sounds.

sources.title: Relative salience of suprasegmental features on judgments of L2 comprehensibility and accentedness
sources.authors: Kang, O.
sources.accents: 11 international teaching assistants (L2 English)
sources.measured: Acoustic analysis of 5-min lectures for speech rate, pauses, stress and pitch range (Praat); comprehensibility/accentedness ratings by 58 US undergraduates
sources.finding: Suprasegmental features independently contribute to accent and comprehensibility judgments; accent ratings best predicted by pitch range and word-stress measures, comprehensibility mostly by speaking rate.

sources.title: Second language speech production: Investigating linguistic correlates of comprehensibility and accentedness for learners at different ability levels
sources.authors: Saito, K.; Trofimovich, P.; Isaacs, T.
sources.accents: 120 Japanese learners of English (beginner, intermediate, advanced)
sources.measured: Segmental, prosodic, temporal, lexical and grammatical analyses of extemporaneous speech vs native-speaker global judgments
sources.finding: Accentedness strongly tied to segmentals and prosody across all proficiency levels; comprehensibility additionally involves vocabulary, rate and grammar. Segmental + prosodic coverage is what an accent score must capture.

sources.title: Intonational variation in urban dialects of English spoken in the British Isles
sources.authors: Grabe, E.
sources.accents: Nine urban British Isles varieties in IViE
sources.measured: F0 contour, pitch accents, boundary tones and speaking style
sources.finding: The IViE project provides directly comparable recordings from London, Cambridge, Cardiff, Leeds, Bradford, Liverpool, Newcastle, Belfast and Dublin, with dialect and style differences in intonation. Exact effect sizes were not verified in the abstract-level source.

sources.title: Intonational variation in four dialects of English: the high rising tune
sources.authors: Fletcher, J.; Grabe, E.; Warren, P.
sources.accents: Four English dialects including New Zealand English
sources.measured: F0-trajectory shape and high-rising terminal alignment
sources.finding: High-rising tunes vary in their phonetic realization across English dialects. The relevant chart is an aligned F0 contour normalized by speaker baseline; no single rise shape should be treated as universal.

sources.title: High Rising Terminals in New Zealand English
sources.authors: Warren, P.
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association
sources.accents: New Zealand English
sources.measured: F0 plots of declarative HRT contours from Wellington recordings
sources.finding: HRTs are a salient, socially evaluated feature of NZE. F0 plots show statement-final rises; the feature overlaps with question intonation, so rise alignment and discourse context matter.

sources.title: The interpretation of prosodic variability in the context of accompanying sociophonetic cues
sources.authors: Warren, P.
sources.accents: New Zealand English
sources.measured: Rise-start alignment, F0 contour and sociophonetic vowel cue interaction
sources.finding: Question rises in younger NZE speakers started earlier than uptalk rises; listeners used this alignment distinction, but interpretation was influenced by the speaker's vowel realization. Prosody interacts with segmental social cues.

sources.title: Prosodic transcription of Glasgow English: an evaluation study of GlaToBI
sources.authors: Mayo, C.; et al.
sources.accents: Glasgow English
sources.measured: Pitch accents, peak alignment and phrase-final contour; GlaToBI labels
sources.finding: Glasgow uses frequent nuclear rises, often followed by a high plateau and final slump. GlaToBI represents the characteristic rise as L*H and handles the plateau-slump differently from standard ToBI.

sources.title: Approaching intonational distance and change
sources.authors: Sullivan, A.
sources.accents: Belfast and Glasgow English
sources.measured: Nuclear-rise peak alignment and scaling in read and Map Task speech
sources.finding: Glasgow and Belfast both use statement rises but differ: Glasgow has earlier H alignment and a final L target, while Belfast has a final H target. These alignment/scaling parameters are directly chartable.

sources.title: Pitch accent types and tonal alignment of the accentual rise in Indian English(es)
sources.authors: Maxwell, O.; Fletcher, J.
sources.accents: Indian English by Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Telugu L1 speakers
sources.measured: H*, L*+H, H*+L and L* pitch accents; peak alignment
sources.finding: All speakers used high and rising accents, but H* vs L*+H distributions differed by L1. Tamil speakers had earlier H alignment; the study reports substantial intra- and inter-speaker variation.

sources.title: Pitch accent in Indian-English teaching discourse
sources.authors: Pickering, L.; Wiltshire, C.
sources.accents: Indian English and American English
sources.measured: F0 and amplitude on lexically accented syllables in teaching discourse
sources.finding: Indian English accented syllables often showed a relative F0 drop without reliable amplitude increase, whereas American English reliably increased both F0 and amplitude in comparable contexts. The authors analyzed IE as pitch-accent-like, though later work challenged the stress-position interpretation.

sources.title: Phonetic stress in Indian English vs. American English
sources.authors: Wiltshire, C.; Moon, R.
sources.accents: Indian English and American English
sources.measured: Pitch, amplitude and duration correlates of stress
sources.finding: The study confirms that IE and AE stressed syllables differ in acoustic realization, but argues that earlier findings of falling pitch may have misidentified the stressed syllable. Stress position may also differ.

sources.title: The prosody of Focus and Givenness in Hindi and Indian English
sources.authors: Féry, C.; Pandey, P.; Kentner, G.
sources.accents: Hindi and Indian English
sources.measured: Prosodic phrasing and prominence in focus/givenness experiments
sources.finding: The authors propose that focus in Hindi and Indian English is realized mainly through enhanced phrasing rather than prominence of the same kind as pitch-accent languages. This is chartable through phrase boundaries and F0/intensity timing, not F0 alone.

sources.title: Quantitative characterizations of speech rhythm: syllable-timing in Singapore English
sources.authors: Low, E. L.; Grabe, E.; Nolan, F.
sources.accents: British English and Singapore English
sources.measured: Vowel-duration variability and vowel quality/reduction
sources.finding: Singapore English had more nearly equal successive vowel durations than British English; reduced vowels were more peripheral in F1/F2. The authors found their vowel variability index more successful than Ramus et al.'s measures for their comparison.

sources.title: Correlates of linguistic rhythm in the speech signal
sources.authors: Ramus, F.; Nespor, M.; Mehler, J.
sources.accents: Eight languages including English, Dutch, French, Spanish and Japanese
sources.measured: %V and deltaC from consonant/vowel segmentation
sources.finding: Measurements of vocalic percentage and consonantal-duration variability supported broad rhythm classes in the eight-language sample. The study used four speakers per language and five sentences per speaker; metrics are chartable but sensitive to segmentation and sample design.

sources.title: Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis
sources.authors: Grabe, E.; Low, E. L.
sources.accents: Multiple languages including English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish
sources.measured: Normalized vocalic nPVI and raw intervocalic rPVI
sources.finding: nPVI/rPVI compare successive interval durations. Their values supported greater durational variability for prototypical stress-timed languages such as English than syllable-timed French/Spanish, but later work finds non-prototypical languages overlap.

sources.title: Calibrating rhythm: First language and second language studies
sources.authors: White, L.; Mattys, S. L.
sources.accents: English, Dutch, Spanish and French; L2 speech
sources.measured: nPVI-V, rPVI-C, deltaV, deltaC, %V, VarcoV and VarcoC
sources.finding: Delta measures were strongly rate-sensitive; VarcoV and nPVI-V discriminated hypothesized rhythm classes, with VarcoV most useful for L1 influence on L2 rhythm. These are normalized duration features suitable for plots, not categorical accent truths.

sources.title: The usefulness of metrics in the quantification of speech rhythm
sources.authors: Arvaniti, A.
sources.accents: English, German, Greek, Italian, Korean and Spanish
sources.measured: DeltaC, %V, PVIs and Varcos under spontaneous, read and controlled elicitation
sources.finding: Across eight speakers per language, classifications were inconsistent; cross-linguistic differences were often nonsignificant, while interspeaker variation and elicitation/syllable-complexity effects were large and sometimes comparable to language effects. Rhythm metrics should be scored cautiously.

sources.title: A comparative account of the suprasegmental and rhythmic features of British English dialects
sources.authors: Ferragne, E.; Pellegrino, F.
sources.accents: 14 British Isles regions in ABI corpus
sources.measured: Automatically extracted duration features and vowel reduction
sources.finding: Celtic-country dialects, especially Irish, were singled out by duration features, but automatic classification showed overlapping rather than crisp dialect categories because of high interspeaker variability. Vowel reduction patterns differed more by gender than dialect.

sources.title: Articulation rate across dialect, age, and gender
sources.authors: Jacewicz, E.; Fox, R. A.; O’Neill, C.; Salmons, J.
sources.accents: Northern Wisconsin and North Carolina American English
sources.measured: Articulation rate in syllables/second; reading vs spontaneous speech
sources.finding: Northern speakers spoke significantly faster than Southern speakers. Mean rates were 3.40 syll/s in reading and 5.12 syll/s in spontaneous speech; age, gender and task also affected rate.

sources.title: Loudness predicts prominence: Fundamental frequency lends little
sources.authors: Kochanski, G.; Grabe, E.; Coleman, J.; Rosner, B.
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Seven British and Irish English dialects
sources.measured: 452-ms syllable-centered windows; loudness, duration, F0 and other measures; classifiers against human prominence judgments
sources.finding: Across seven dialects and three styles, loudness and duration were primary prominence cues; F0 played a minor role. A useful game score should not equate pitch movement with prominence by itself.

sources.title: Voice quality in Glaswegian
sources.authors: Stuart-Smith, J.
sources.accents: Glaswegian English
sources.measured: Vocal Profile Analysis of conversational/read speech from 32 socially stratified speakers
sources.finding: The study found few universal stereotypes but clear social differences in voice-quality settings; middle-class profiles were largely characterized by absence of typical working-class settings. Voice quality can carry local social information, but is not a simple accent label.

sources.title: Creaky voice: A new feminine voice quality for young urban-oriented upwardly mobile American women?
sources.authors: Yuasa, I. P.
sources.accents: Northern and Californian American English; Japanese comparison
sources.measured: Conversational creak frequency and matched-guise judgments
sources.finding: Young California American women used creaky voice more frequently than comparable American men and Japanese women in the sample. Listeners associated the voice with social meanings such as informal, educated and urban-oriented; this is social-indexical rather than a pure regional cue.

sources.title: Gender differences in the acoustic realization of creaky voice
sources.authors: Podesva, R. J.; Szakay, A. (per Crossref; the summariser had listed Esposito, C.)
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Northern California English
sources.measured: H1-H2 at vowel midpoints in 362,429 tokens from 30 speakers
sources.finding: H1-H2 was significantly lower for female speakers, indicating greater creak, although H1-H2 under-captures some creak. Linguistic factors including F0, intensity, stress and phrase position also affected the measure.
sources.note: Published JASA conference abstract; token counts quoted here are UNVERIFIED.

sources.title: Laver’s phonetic description of voice quality
sources.authors: Laver, J.
sources.accents: General voice-quality theory
sources.measured: Phonatory, supralaryngeal and tension settings; articulatory settings
sources.finding: Provides the descriptive framework for voice quality as recurring articulatory/phonatory settings rather than segment-only properties. Modern acoustic proxies include spectral tilt, CPP and periodicity, but they are not one-to-one with Laver's settings.

sources.title: YIN, a fundamental frequency estimator for speech and music
sources.authors: de Cheveigné, A.; Kawahara, H.
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Speech and music; pitch tracking
sources.measured: Autocorrelation-based F0 estimation with error-prevention modifications
sources.finding: YIN reported error rates about three times lower than the best competing methods in its laryngograph-evaluated database. It is efficient and low-latency, but browser use still needs voicing confidence and noise handling.

sources.title: pYIN: A fundamental frequency estimator using probabilistic threshold distributions
sources.authors: Mauch, M.; Dixon, S.
sources.accents: Speech pitch tracking
sources.measured: Multiple YIN candidates, probabilistic thresholds and HMM/Viterbi smoothing
sources.finding: pYIN improves on framewise YIN by preserving multiple candidates and using temporal smoothing; the authors report substantially higher recall and precision with low added computational complexity. It is appropriate for contour extraction but not itself evidence that accents differ.

sources.title: CREPE: A Convolutional Representation for Pitch Estimation
sources.authors: Kim, J. W.; Salamon, J.; Li, P.; Bello, J. P.
sources.accents: Monophonic speech pitch tracking
sources.measured: Waveform convolutional neural network; noise robustness
sources.finding: CREPE matched or exceeded pYIN and was reported as more noise-robust; it maintained over 90% raw pitch accuracy at a strict 10-cent threshold in the reported evaluation. This is a tracker benchmark, not an accent-classification result.

sources.title: A comparison of vowel normalization procedures for language variation research
sources.authors: Adank, P.; Smits, R.; van Hout, R.
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Dutch regional varieties
sources.measured: F0 and F1-F3; vowel-intrinsic/extrinsic and formant-intrinsic/extrinsic normalization
sources.finding: Across 80 female and 80 male Dutch talkers, vowel-extrinsic methods generally preserved regional information better than vowel-intrinsic methods; formant-intrinsic methods outperformed formant-extrinsic alternatives.

sources.title: Comparing vowel formant normalization methods
sources.authors: Flynn, N.; Foulkes, P.
sources.accents: English speakers, sociophonetic comparison
sources.measured: 20 normalization methods; F1-F2 vowel-space equalization and alignment
sources.finding: Vowel-extrinsic, formant-intrinsic, speaker-intrinsic methods performed best overall; vowel-intrinsic transformations performed poorly, though better than raw Hz.

sources.title: Evaluation of a technique for improving the mapping of multiple speakers’ vowel spaces in the F1-F2 plane
sources.authors: Watt, D.; Fabricius, A.
sources.venue: Leeds Working Papers in Linguistics and Phonetics
sources.accents: English speakers
sources.measured: F1/F2; Watt-Fabricius centroid normalization
sources.finding: Centroid-based ratios improved agreement in vowel-triangle area and overlap compared with linear Hz and z/Bark mappings. Chart: normalized F1-F2 vowel triangles.

sources.title: The Atlas of North American English
sources.authors: Labov, W.; Ash, S.; Boberg, C.
sources.accents: North American English, US and Canada
sources.measured: Telephone survey; vowel systems, mergers, shifts, diphthong movement
sources.finding: Provides the first broad acoustic account of North American vowel systems and maps regional patterns including the Northern Cities Shift, low-back merger, and /uw, ow, aw/ fronting. Exact feature values vary by region and speaker.

sources.title: The third dialect of English: Some Canadian evidence
sources.authors: Clarke, S.; Elms, F.; Youssef, A.
sources.accents: Canadian English
sources.measured: Lax-vowel F1/F2 shifts; cot-caught merger; back-vowel fronting
sources.finding: Canadian English lax vowels showed a substantial shift, with /æ/ retraction and lowering of /ɛ/ and /ɪ/ discussed in relation to the low-back merger; following voicing and manner and speaker gender conditioned outcomes.

sources.title: Regional phonetic differentiation in Standard Canadian English
sources.authors: Boberg, C.
sources.accents: Six Canadian regions
sources.measured: Acoustic vowel and phonetic variables in 86 young educated speakers
sources.finding: The study proposed six phonetic regions of Standard Canadian English: British Columbia, Prairies, Ontario, Quebec, Maritimes, and Newfoundland, refining the Atlas's three-region account.

sources.title: The Canadian Shift in Toronto
sources.authors: Hoffman, M.; Walker, J.
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association
sources.accents: Mainstream Toronto English
sources.measured: Apparent-time acoustic F1/F2 of /ɪ, ɛ, æ/ and low-back vowels
sources.finding: Toronto data showed lowering and retraction of nonhigh front lax vowels, with retraction more prominent in recent change; the authors found no evidence for a classic chain shift and proposed a parallel shift.

sources.title: Exploring the Vowel Space of Multicultural Toronto English
sources.authors: Denis, D.; Elango, V.; Nor Kamal, N. S.; Prashar, S.; Velasco, M.
sources.accents: Multicultural Toronto English
sources.measured: GOOSE fronting, Canadian Vowel Shift, Canadian raising, ban/bag tensing, GOAT monophthongization
sources.finding: Young Greater Toronto Area speakers showed substantial interspeaker variability and little coherent covariation across five vocalic phenomena, consistent with a variable multiethnolect repertoire rather than one uniform vowel system.

sources.title: Contact, the feature pool and the speech community: the emergence of Multicultural London English
sources.authors: Cheshire, J.; Kerswill, P.; Fox, S.; Torgersen, E.
sources.accents: Multicultural London English
sources.measured: Diphthongs, GOOSE-fronting and other sociophonetic variables across age/community
sources.finding: MLE innovations included diphthong changes; adolescent incrementation was strongest for global changes such as BE LIKE and GOOSE-fronting, while other features followed community-internal patterns.

sources.title: Acoustic and durational properties of Indian English vowels
sources.authors: Maxwell, O.; Fletcher, J.
sources.accents: Indian English by Hindi and Punjabi L1 speakers
sources.measured: Monophthong F1/F2, vowel duration, tense-lax contrasts and diphthongs
sources.finding: Hindi- and Punjabi-background Indian English speakers showed a modified vowel inventory; some tense-lax contrasts were realized through quality and duration, others through duration alone. Diphthongs also showed L1-linked variation.

sources.title: The effects of native language on Indian English sounds and timing patterns
sources.authors: Sirsa, H.; Redford, M. A.
sources.accents: Indian English by Hindi and Telugu L1 speakers
sources.measured: Vowels, obstruent consonants, retroflex/stop-related measures and temporal patterns; listener judgments
sources.finding: Naive listeners distinguished Hindi and Telugu phrases well, while experienced listeners distinguished IE speaker backgrounds; acoustic measures separated native languages, but only three measures separated the IE groups. This warns against treating “Indian English” as acoustically uniform.

sources.title: An acoustic study of voiceless stops in Indian English
sources.authors: UNVERIFIED author list; et al.
sources.accents: Indian English and British English
sources.measured: VOT in word-initial and post-/s/ bilabial and dorsal voiceless stops
sources.finding: Across 102 bilingual Indian English speakers and 28 British English speakers, Indian English stops had short positive VOT in both contexts, while British English distinguished the contexts with aspiration-related VOT differences; vowel-onset F0 did not differ significantly by context.

sources.title: The social stratification of tongue shape for postvocalic /r/ in Scottish English
sources.authors: Lawson, E.; Scobbie, J. M.; Stuart-Smith, J.
sources.accents: Scottish English
sources.measured: Ultrasound tongue imaging of CVr; bunched vs tongue-tip/front raised articulations; auditory rhoticity
sources.finding: Middle-class speakers used more bunched /r/, while working-class speakers used more tongue-tip/front-raised variants. Articulatory variants correlated with a socially stratified strong-to-weak rhotic continuum.

sources.title: Voice quality and coda /r/ in Glasgow English in the early 20th century
sources.authors: Stuart-Smith, J.; Lawson, E.; Scobbie, J. M.
sources.accents: Historical Glasgow English
sources.measured: Acoustic F3 and auditory /r/, with voice-quality control
sources.finding: Initial F3 increase suggested weakening /r/, but voice-quality change explained much of the shift; after controlling voice quality, moderate changes remained mainly for females. F3 alone is therefore not a safe rhoticity score.

sources.title: ‘Talkin’ Jockney’? Variation and change in Glaswegian accent
sources.authors: Stuart-Smith, J.; Timmins, C.; Tweedie, F.
sources.accents: Glaswegian English
sources.measured: Eight consonantal variables in read and spontaneous speech from 32 speakers
sources.finding: Working-class adolescents increased non-local TH-fronting and reduced expected Scottish postvocalic /r/; middle-class speakers maintained more traditional Scottish features. The study used multivariate social-pattern analysis rather than one acoustic cue.

sources.title: L-vocalisation as a natural phenomenon: explorations in sociophonology
sources.authors: Johnson, W.; Britain, D.
sources.accents: South-eastern British and other English varieties
sources.measured: Dark /l/ vocalization in syllable codas; sociophonetic distribution
sources.finding: Coda /l/ vocalization is widespread in south-eastern Britain and occurs in other English varieties. The feature can be treated as a categorical/gradient coda consonant variable, but its social distribution is location-dependent.

sources.title: Vowel duration in Scottish English speaking children
sources.authors: Scobbie, J. M.; Hewlett, N.; Turk, A.
sources.accents: Scottish English children
sources.measured: Duration of /i/ and /u/ in Scottish Vowel Length Rule and voicing contexts
sources.finding: In seven children aged 6–9, four showed a robust Scottish Vowel Length pattern with a minimal voicing effect; children with two non-Scottish parents showed absent or weaker patterns.

sources.title: Cross-dialectal variation in formant dynamics of American English vowels
sources.authors: Fox, R. A.; Jacewicz, E.
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Western North Carolina, Central Ohio, Southern Wisconsin English
sources.measured: F1/F2 trajectories, duration, vector/trajectory length and spectral rate for five vowels; 48 women, 1,920 utterances
sources.finding: Dialect was a strong source of variation in dynamic vowel spectral change. Position and movement in F1-F2, duration, trajectory length (but not vector length), and spectral rate effectively characterized regional differences.

sources.title: The Mobile Phone Effect on vowel formants
sources.authors: Byrne, C.; Foulkes, P.
sources.venue: International Journal of Speech, Language and the Law
sources.accents: English speakers; mobile transmission
sources.measured: F1-F3 from simultaneous direct and mobile recordings of 12 speakers
sources.finding: Mobile transmission raised F1 by 29% on average relative to direct recordings; F2 was generally not significantly affected and F3 was mostly stable except for some high-F3 speakers. Raw F1 comparisons across phones are unsafe.

sources.title: How Reliable Are Phonetic Data Collected Remotely?
sources.authors: UNVERIFIED author list; et al.
sources.accents: English speech recorded on smartphones, laptops and Zoom
sources.measured: Duration, F0, F1/F2+, spectral moments and voice quality across devices, rooms and cloud recording
sources.finding: Devices were comparable for F0 and F1, but differed substantially for F2+, spectral moments and voice-quality measures. Local recording was reliable for duration; cloud recording was not. Smartphone/Zoom recordings were more suitable for prosody than fine segmental contrasts.

sources.title: Examining recording quality from two methods of remote data collection in a study of vowel reduction
sources.authors: Morrison, G. S.; et al.
sources.accents: English vowel reduction; smartphone and web recordings
sources.measured: Relative duration, Euclidean distance, Pillai scores and normalized stressed/unstressed formants
sources.finding: Temporal measures and Pillai scores were unaffected by recording method; Euclidean distance and normalized formants showed some significant changes but broadly tracked lab results. Smartphone recording affected low/back vowels more strongly.

sources.title: Hanani, Russell and Carey 2011 accent classification
sources.authors: Hanani, A.; Russell, M.; Carey, M.
sources.accents: 14 regional accents of British English in ABI corpus
sources.measured: ACCDIST and acoustic language-identification systems; speaker-independent evaluation
sources.finding: Text-dependent ACCDIST reached 95.18% accuracy; a conventional text-independent acoustic system reached 89.6% when phone-sequence information was added; human listeners reached 58.25% in the reported task. These are corpus results, not phone-mic guarantees.

sources.title: Montreal Forced Aligner: Trainable Text-Speech Alignment Using Kaldi
sources.authors: McAuliffe, M.; Socolof, M.; Mihuc, S.; Wagner, M.; Sonderegger, M.
sources.accents: Any (used here with english_us_arpa models for all VCTK speakers)
sources.measured: Forced phone/word alignment
sources.finding: Used in this repo to find vowel/consonant boundaries for VCTK. Alignment locates phones; it does not judge accent.

sources.title: Introducing Parselmouth: A Python interface to Praat
sources.authors: Jadoul, Y.; Thompson, B.; de Boer, B.
sources.accents: n/a
sources.measured: Praat pitch and formant tracking from Python
sources.finding: Used in this repo for F0 (autocorrelation) and Burg formant tracking.

sources.title: Classification of Russian Vowels Spoken by Different Speakers
sources.authors: Lobanov, B. M.
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
sources.accents: Russian (method paper)
sources.measured: Speaker z-score normalisation of formants
sources.finding: Origin of Lobanov normalisation (z-score F1/F2 per speaker), which this repo uses for every vowel chart and vowel classifier.

sources.title: WavLM: Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pre-Training for Full Stack Speech Processing
sources.authors: Chen, S.; Wang, C.; Chen, Z.; Wu, Y.; Liu, S.; Chen, Z.; et al.
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing
sources.accents: n/a
sources.measured: Self-supervised speech representations
sources.finding: microsoft/wavlm-base-plus is one of the two embedding models tested layer-by-layer in this repo.

sources.title: wav2vec 2.0: A Framework for Self-Supervised Learning of Speech Representations
sources.authors: Baevski, A.; Zhou, H.; Mohamed, A.; Auli, M.
sources.accents: n/a
sources.measured: Self-supervised speech representations
sources.finding: facebook/wav2vec2-base is the second embedding model tested layer-by-layer in this repo.
